nameStory: The brown-toothed crust fungus gets its name from its distinctive spore-bearing surface that looks like tiny brown teeth or spines pointing downward. Unlike many fungi that have gills or pores, this species produces its spores from these tooth-like projections, making it easy to remember once you've seen it up close.
description: This fungus forms thin, crusty patches that spread across dead wood like a rough, textured skin. The surface is covered with small, brownish tooth-like projections that point downward, giving it a fuzzy or bristly appearance. It typically grows in patches ranging from a few inches to over a foot across, hugging tightly to its wooden host without forming a traditional mushroom shape.

idTips.label: Teeth
idTips.description: Small brown spines or teeth project downward from the surface, feeling slightly rough to the touch like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, crusty patches that spread across wood surfaces without a stem or cap, resembling textured paint

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Overall brownish to olive-brown coloration, sometimes with darker brown teeth and lighter margins

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels firm and leathery when fresh, becoming more brittle when dry, with a slightly fuzzy surface from the protruding teeth

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on dead hardwood, particularly favoring oak, maple, and beech logs and branches

habitat: Look for this fungus on dead hardwood logs, fallen branches, and stumps in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. It particularly favors oak, maple, and beech wood in moist woodland areas. You'll often find it on the undersides of logs or on vertical surfaces where moisture tends to collect.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins as moisture increases, appearing as thin, developing patches on dead wood. Look for the characteristic teeth starting to emerge.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the fungus expands rapidly after rain events. Teeth are well-developed and the brown coloration is most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Continues active growth through autumn rains. Mature specimens are easy to spot as leaves fall and expose more dead wood.
seasonality.winter: Persists on wood but becomes dormant and more brittle. Old specimens may still be visible but are less distinct.

funFact: This fungus can actually help forensic investigators determine how long wood has been dead, since it colonizes deadwood in predictable patterns and timeframes!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other brown crust fungi, but the downward-pointing teeth are the giveaway - poke gently with your finger and you'll feel the spiky texture that other smooth crust fungi lack. Memory trick: 'Brown teeth bite down' - the teeth always point downward.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Hydnoporia combines 'hydno' meaning tooth-like (from Greek) and 'poria' referring to pores, reflecting how this group bridges the gap between toothed fungi and pore fungi in terms of spore-bearing structures.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the glue crust fungus which has a smooth surface, brown-toothed crust always has those distinctive downward-pointing teeth. Willow glue tends to be more yellowish-brown and lacks the prominent teeth, growing mainly on willow wood rather than the diverse hardwoods this species prefers.
